Global Dialogue on AI Governance
3–4 May 2027 | New York
As artificial intelligence advances rapidly, international cooperation on its governance is more important than ever. The Global Dialogue on AI Governance brings governments and stakeholders from every region together for inclusive discussions informed by independent science.
Sign up for updates
Meet the 2027 Co-Chairs
On 16 October 2026, the President of the General Assembly appointed two Permanent Representatives as Co-Chairs of the 2027 Dialogue, in line with General Assembly resolution 79/325.

H.E. Mr. Jihoon Cha

The inaugural Global Dialogue on AI Governance in Geneva, 6–7 July 2026. UN Photo/Elma Okic
About the Dialogue
Established by General Assembly resolution 79/325, adopted by consensus on 26 August 2025, the Dialogue builds directly on the Global Digital Compact. It is the first global platform of its kind dedicated to AI governance and is open to all Member States.
Each year, it brings governments together with the private sector, civil society, academia and the technical community to exchange best practices, foster common approaches and help ensure AI governance reflects the priorities of all countries.
The 2027 Dialogue will take place back-to-back with the
12th Multi-stakeholder Forum on Science, Technology and Innovation for the Sustainable Development Goals
Independent science informing the Dialogue
The Independent International Scientific Panel on AI provides evidence-based assessments of AI's opportunities, risks and impacts. The Panel's next annual report will inform the 2027 Dialogue.
Learn more about the Scientific Panel
The Independent International Scientific Panel on AI presents its Preliminary Report at the Global Dialogue on AI Governance in Geneva on 6 July 2026. UN Photo/Elma Okic
2026 Dialogue: Geneva
The inaugural Global Dialogue on AI Governance was held in Geneva on 6 and 7 July 2026. Delegations from 163 countries took part, alongside representatives of the private sector, civil society, academia and the technical community. The 2026 Dialogue was co-chaired by H.E. Ms. Egriselda López, Permanent Representative of El Salvador, and H.E. Mr. Rein Tammsaar, Permanent Representative of Estonia.

Established with Resolution A/RES/79/325 on 26 August 2025, the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI serves as the first global scientific body on Artificial Intelligence (AI), bringing together leading experts to assess how AI is transforming our lives.
In a world where AI is racing ahead, this Panel will provide what’s been missing – rigorous, independent scientific insight.
António Guterres, United Nations Secretary-General
Background
The Global Digital Compact (
A/RES/79/1
), adopted at the 2024 Summit of the Future, set out a shared vision for an open, safe, and inclusive digital future. Among its commitments was the creation of an Independent International Scientific Panel on AI to advance scientific understanding and ensure that international deliberations are informed by the best available evidence.
The United Nations General Assembly established the
Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence
in Resolution

, following intergovernmental negotiations and broad consultations with diverse stakeholders. Details of the process and previous revisions of the resolution can be found

Questions and Answers about GIZ
What is GIZ?
The Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) GmbH is a federal enterprise with worldwide operations. It supports the German Federal Government and many other public and private clients in achieving their goals in international cooperation for sustainable development and international education work. Together with its partners, GIZ has been developing effective solutions that offer people better prospects and improve their living conditions for more than 50 years.
GIZ is wholly owned by the German Federal Government. As a shareholder, the Federal Government is represented by the German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ) and the German Ministry of Finance (BMF).
How does GIZ work?
We work in almost 120 countries worldwide. All projects are based on a specific mandate – for example from the German Federal Government, national and international clients or the private sector.
We offer a wide range of services: we advise policy-makers and the private sector locally in our partner countries, for example on economic development and employment promotion, energy and the environment and peace and security. Our work focuses on developing and strengthening the capacities of individuals, organisations and governments. We see this as the key to sustainable development – and sustainability is the principle that guides our actions and core business. A specific example is the work we do to support countries in driving digital transformation and implementing measures to counter disinformation. We develop strategies for fair skilled labour migration, manage construction and infrastructure projects and assist people in dealing with the impacts of climate change.
Who commissions GIZ?
Our work is financed by public and private funds. We use these funds in a targeted manner to achieve the best possible results. Our main commissioning party is the German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ). In 2025, around EUR 3.2 billion of our business volume was commissioned by BMZ. A further approx. EUR 443 million was commissioned by other German public contracting authorities, such as the German Federal Ministry of the Environment, Climate Action, Nature Conservation and Nuclear Safety (BMUKN) and the German Federal Foreign Office. We also support the federal states in implementing international development cooperation activities.
We also work for international clients such as the European Union, various UN organisations and foundations. National governments from all over the world, as well as the private sector, also commission us directly.
Who does GIZ work with?
We work with a host of partners around the globe. Stable partnerships bring together interests between Germany, Europe and our partner countries and are essential for our work. After all, change can be achieved only if we work together.
We cooperate with international and regional organisations and with stakeholders from civil society and the scientific and academic community. We work with local partners – often with the relevant national ministries, but also with municipalities and local organisations. In Germany, we maintain close contact with public institutions, foundations, associations and KfW Development Bank.

Under the theme “Shaping a Global AI Future Through Science, Policy, and Capacity,” the day brought together governments, the UN system, industry, academia, civil society and the technical community to advance implementation of the Global Digital Compact. Opening the day, Under-Secretary-General and Special Envoy for Digital and Emerging Technologies Amandeep Gill framed the theme through three verbs: to know, to choose and to act. “AI is not an uncontrollable force of nature,” he said. “It is built by humans. It can be steered by humans.” More than 1,000 people attended Digital Cooperation Day, with 80 speakers across 18 sessions. In-person and remote participation reached 105 countries, with more than 4,700 remote livestream views. About the International AI Safety Report
The International AI Safety Report is the world's first comprehensive review of the latest science on the capabilities and risks of general-purpose AI systems. The work was overseen by an international Expert Advisory Panel nominated by over 30 countries and intergovernmental organisations. Written by over 100 independent experts and led by Turing Award winner Yoshua Bengio, it represents the largest international collaboration on AI safety research to date. The Report provides decision-makers in government and beyond with a shared and authorative global picture of AI's risks and impacts.
3 February 2026
Annual Report
International AI Safety Report 2026
The second International AI Safety Report, published in February 2026, is the next iteration of the comprehensive review of latest scientific research on the capabilities and risks of general-purpose AI systems. Led by Turing Award winner Yoshua Bengio and authored by over 100 AI experts, the report is backed by over 30 countries and international organisations. It represents the largest global collaboration on AI safety to date.
Translated versions in the other 5 official UN languages can be found under the 'More Languages' button. The 'Extended Summary for Policymakers' can be found on the main 'Publications' page.
3 February 2026
Summary
2026 Report: Extended Summary for Policymakers
The Extended Summary for Policymakers provides a detailed (20 page) summary of the full 2026 Report. It includes the Report’s key findings and figures, concrete examples and a list of notable developments since the 2025 edition. It is structured around three central questions: what can general-purpose AI do today, what emerging risks does it pose, and how can those risks be mitigated?
Translated versions in the other 5 official UN languages can be found under the 'More Languages' button.
3 February 2026
Summary
2026 Report: Executive Summary
The Executive Summary offers a concise three-page overview of the 2026 Report’s core findings on general-purpose AI capabilities, emerging risks, and risk management approaches. It covers how AI capabilities are advancing, what real-world evidence is emerging for key risks, and progress and remaining limitations in technical, institutional, and societal risk management measures.
25 November 2025
Key update
Second Key Update: Technical Safeguards and Risk Management
This Key Update examines developments in technical approaches to general-purpose AI risk management, from training models to refuse harmful requests to watermarking AI-generated content. Since the publication of the 2025 International AI Safety Report, the number of companies publishing Frontier AI Safety Frameworks has more than doubled, and researchers have refined techniques for training safer models and detecting AI-generated content. However, significant gaps remain: sophisticated attackers can often bypass current defences, and the real-world effectiveness of many safeguards is uncertain.

Since its founding at the dawn of the atomic age, UNESCO has helped societies navigate and manage the transformative power of technology – to the benefit of all.
Today, in an era shaped by Artificial Intelligence (AI) and related breakthrough innovations, UNESCO continues the critical work of ensuring these emerging technologies are developed and deployed in service of equity, opportunity, and inclusivity.
Video series: 7 minutes to understand AI
© shutterstock.com / 3rdtimeluckystudio
Our impact
How UNESCO is shaping an ethical digital future.
Green Digital Transformation
We foster global collaboration to make AI more sustainable, inclusive, and resilient for everyone.
Digital transformation
We promote a human-centered digital transformation, wherein AI, data, and open solutions build capacity, foster inclusion, protect diversity, and drive sustainable, rights-based innovation.
Quantum computing
We are helping the world prepare for the quantum revolution, wherein quantum mechanics helps solve problems too complex for today’s computers, in areas like medicine, encryption, and materials science.
Neurotechnology
We are developing ethical frameworks to ensure these technologies fulfill their promise in health while upholding equity, mental privacy, freedom of thought, and protection of the most vulnerable.
Natural science
We leverage AI to advance innovative, science-based solutions for sustainable development – from managing water and biodiversity to reducing disaster risks and strengthening climate resilience.
Information integrity
Algorithms and generative AI are reshaping how people access and trust information, with major effects on journalism, expression, and rights. We foster media literacy and inform digital platform governance.
Culture
As AI transforms how culture is created, accessed, managed, and experienced, UNESCO works to ensure AI’s development and use protect and promote cultural diversity, creativity, and access for all.
Gender
New technologies risk widening gender gaps, especially when AI learns from biased data. UNESCO’s work on AI and gender guides policymakers and innovators to close these divides.
Education
We convene leaders, experts, and innovators to address the impact of AI and technology in education, promoting human-centered, inclusive, and equitable approaches to the benefit of all learners.
Building standards together: emerging technology ethics
UNESCO’s normative recommendations guide the ethical use of technologies, helping ensure they respect human rights, promote fairness, and benefit everyone.
Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology
The 2025 UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology sets global principles to ensure neurotechnology is developed and used in ways that respect human rights, dignity, and societal well-being.
Recommendation on the Ethics of AI
In 2021, UNESCO adopted the Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, guiding its work and helping Member States develop ethically aligned AI policies and capacities.
Policy Development: Readiness Assessment Methodology (RAMs)
UNESCO helps Member States evaluate their readiness for the AI transformation through its Readiness Assessment Methodology (RAM) program, which helps policymakers identify their policy gaps and develop their national policies and strategies toward the development and deployment of these transformative technologies.
As of October 2025, over 75 countries from five continents have initiated or completed to RAM assessments, and policymakers worldwide are further able to draw on the Technology Policy Assistance Facility, developed in cooperation with the South African G20 Presidency.
Readiness Assessment Methodology
Technology Policy Assistance Facility
© SeventyFour / Shutterstock.com
Key initiatives
G20 Technology Policy Assistance Facility
A G20-backed platform that helps policymakers and stakeholders research, design, and implement ethical, inclusive, and future-ready technology and AI policies.
Global AI Ethics and Governance Observatory
The Observatory supports global stakeholders in promoting ethical and responsible AI through research, tools, and best practices.
Readiness Assessment Methodology (RAM)
The RAM program helps governments identify and address gaps in their AI policies, strategies, and legislation, so that AI is deployed ethically and responsibly to the benefit of their their citizens.
Internet Universality Indicators
This tool helps countries assess their Internet landscape, guide evidence-based policies, and foster inclusive, future-ready digital governance.
UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance
The UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance brings together Member States and stakeholders to engage in the meaningful global conversation on AI that the world needs.
Coordinated by UNESCO and the ITU as the joint UN Secretariat, the Dialogue—mandated by the General Assembly—aims to ensure that AI governance reflects the priorities of all nations, not just the most technologically advanced. International cooperation on AI governance is essential to ensure that AI development benefits all of us.

About the International AI Safety Report
The International AI Safety Report is the world's first comprehensive review of the latest science on the capabilities and risks of general-purpose AI systems. The work was overseen by an international Expert Advisory Panel nominated by over 30 countries and intergovernmental organisations. Written by over 100 independent experts and led by Turing Award winner Yoshua Bengio, it represents the largest international collaboration on AI safety research to date. The Report provides decision-makers in government and beyond with a shared and authorative global picture of AI's risks and impacts.

Questions and Answers about GIZ
What is GIZ?
The Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) GmbH is a federal enterprise with worldwide operations. It supports the German Federal Government and many other public and private clients in achieving their goals in international cooperation for sustainable development and international education work. Together with its partners, GIZ has been developing effective solutions that offer people better prospects and improve their living conditions for more than 50 years.
GIZ is wholly owned by the German Federal Government. As a shareholder, the Federal Government is represented by the German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ) and the German Ministry of Finance (BMF).
How does GIZ work?
We work in almost 120 countries worldwide. All projects are based on a specific mandate – for example from the German Federal Government, national and international clients or the private sector.
We offer a wide range of services: we advise policy-makers and the private sector locally in our partner countries, for example on economic development and employment promotion, energy and the environment and peace and security. Our work focuses on developing and strengthening the capacities of individuals, organisations and governments. We see this as the key to sustainable development – and sustainability is the principle that guides our actions and core business. A specific example is the work we do to support countries in driving digital transformation and implementing measures to counter disinformation. We develop strategies for fair skilled labour migration, manage construction and infrastructure projects and assist people in dealing with the impacts of climate change.
Who commissions GIZ?
Our work is financed by public and private funds. We use these funds in a targeted manner to achieve the best possible results. Our main commissioning party is the German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ). In 2025, around EUR 3.2 billion of our business volume was commissioned by BMZ. A further approx. EUR 443 million was commissioned by other German public contracting authorities, such as the German Federal Ministry of the Environment, Climate Action, Nature Conservation and Nuclear Safety (BMUKN) and the German Federal Foreign Office. We also support the federal states in implementing international development cooperation activities.
We also work for international clients such as the European Union, various UN organisations and foundations. National governments from all over the world, as well as the private sector, also commission us directly.
Who does GIZ work with?
We work with a host of partners around the globe. Stable partnerships bring together interests between Germany, Europe and our partner countries and are essential for our work. After all, change can be achieved only if we work together.
We cooperate with international and regional organisations and with stakeholders from civil society and the scientific and academic community. We work with local partners – often with the relevant national ministries, but also with municipalities and local organisations. In Germany, we maintain close contact with public institutions, foundations, associations and KfW Development Bank.
Furthermore, cooperation with the private sector is becoming more and more important. In partnership with us, companies can steer their activities so that their success also results in improved living conditions for people locally. We pave the way for more private involvement in our countries of assignment by advising them on the right framework conditions and making use of networks to bring potential partners together. Take hydrogen, for example: we provide advice on the market ramp-up of green hydrogen in countries such as Brazil, South Africa and Morocco. This supports local people and also opens doors for German businesses, helps the climate and makes an important contribution to Germany’s energy security.
What values guide GIZ?
We work to shape a future worth living around the world. In doing so, our actions are guided by the principle of sustainability. We firmly believe that social responsibility, ecological balance and economic capacity must go hand in hand if current and future generations are to live safe, secure and dignified lives. As a federal enterprise, we are also guided by the principles upheld in German society. We promote respect for human rights, equal opportunities and integrity. At the same time, we support the rule of law and the political participation of the population, and are also committed to fairness within our own company.
What relevance does GIZ's work have for Germany?
International cooperation is in the
interests of Germany
and Europe. It promotes peace, security and prosperity worldwide – including here at home. Our work is not only effective locally for every single person we support, but also in the almost 120 countries in which we operate, as it creates more stable conditions. Moreover, what we achieve in the rest of the world also has an impact here in Germany and Europe. For example, we help companies to open up new markets, secure jobs and attract skilled labour, we create prospects and reduce the root causes of displacement, and we ensure energy security and stable raw material supply chains. As an export nation, Germany is particularly dependent on stable partnerships and international cooperation to maintain its own prosperity. Our contribution to this is significant.
Is GIZ a public-benefit organisation?
GIZ is a corporation in the legal form of a limited liability company under German law (GmbH), which is recognised as having a public-benefit status due to its corporate purpose. It is not our aim to maximise financial profit. We think in an entrepreneurial way and act cost-effectively; however, we are not profit-driven. We focus on supporting public welfare as part of our corporate purpose.
We generate the majority of our revenue (almost EUR 4 billion in 2025) through the German federal government and other public-sector clients in Germany. These commissions are exempt from corporation and trade tax. Commissions from other clients, such as the European Commission, are taxed in accordance with German income tax regulations. However, even with these commissions, GIZ does not focus on making a profit. GIZ works on a cost-covering basis and also retains a small risk premium for these commissions to cover the entrepreneurial risk. Surplus profits are used for further international cooperation projects in line with the company’s purpose.
What is GIZ's business volume?
In 2025, GIZ’s business volume was almost EUR 4 billion. Around EUR 3.7 billion of this was commissioned by federal ministries and other public sector clients in Germany. Business worth EUR 295 million was commissioned and financed by international clients from industrialised, emerging and developing countries.
Who manages GIZ?
GIZ is managed by a three-person
Management Board
. Thorsten Schäfer-Gümbel is Chair of the Management Board. The other members are Ingrid-Gabriela Hoven and Anna Sophie Herken.
When was GIZ established?
GIZ was established on 1 January 2011 as the result of a merger between three organisations: Deutsche Gesellschaft für Technische Zusammenarbeit (GTZ) GmbH, the German Development Service (DED) gGmbH and Internationale Weiterbildung und Entwicklung gGmbH (InWEnt; Capacity Building International, Germany).
Where is GIZ based?
GIZ has two registered offices in Germany: one in Bonn and one in Eschborn, near Frankfurt am Main.
How many employees does GIZ have?
As at 31 December 2025, a total of 23,787 people were working for GIZ in almost 120 countries – with 5,640 employed in Germany and 2,324 seconded abroad. 15,823 people worked as local staff in the partner countries. Overall, almost two thirds of GIZ employees work abroad. In 2025, GIZ’s workforce also included 184 development workers.

About the Dialogue
Established by General Assembly resolution 79/325, adopted by consensus on 26 August 2025, the Dialogue builds directly on the Global Digital Compact. It is the first global platform of its kind dedicated to AI governance and is open to all Member States.
Each year, it brings governments together with the private sector, civil society, academia and the technical community to exchange best practices, foster common approaches and help ensure AI governance reflects the priorities of all countries.
The 2027 Dialogue will take place back-to-back with the
12th Multi-stakeholder Forum on Science, Technology and Innovation for the Sustainable Development Goals
Independent science informing the Dialogue
The Independent International Scientific Panel on AI provides evidence-based assessments of AI's opportunities, risks and impacts. The Panel's next annual report will inform the 2027 Dialogue.

2026 Dialogue: Geneva
The inaugural Global Dialogue on AI Governance was held in Geneva on 6 and 7 July 2026. Delegations from 163 countries took part, alongside representatives of the private sector, civil society, academia and the technical community. The 2026 Dialogue was co-chaired by H.E. Ms. Egriselda López, Permanent Representative of El Salvador, and H.E. Mr. Rein Tammsaar, Permanent Representative of Estonia.

Since its founding at the dawn of the atomic age, UNESCO has helped societies navigate and manage the transformative power of technology – to the benefit of all.
Today, in an era shaped by Artificial Intelligence (AI) and related breakthrough innovations, UNESCO continues the critical work of ensuring these emerging technologies are developed and deployed in service of equity, opportunity, and inclusivity.

Our impact
How UNESCO is shaping an ethical digital future.
Green Digital Transformation
We foster global collaboration to make AI more sustainable, inclusive, and resilient for everyone.
Digital transformation
We promote a human-centered digital transformation, wherein AI, data, and open solutions build capacity, foster inclusion, protect diversity, and drive sustainable, rights-based innovation.
Quantum computing
We are helping the world prepare for the quantum revolution, wherein quantum mechanics helps solve problems too complex for today’s computers, in areas like medicine, encryption, and materials science.
Neurotechnology
We are developing ethical frameworks to ensure these technologies fulfill their promise in health while upholding equity, mental privacy, freedom of thought, and protection of the most vulnerable.
Natural science
We leverage AI to advance innovative, science-based solutions for sustainable development – from managing water and biodiversity to reducing disaster risks and strengthening climate resilience.
Information integrity
Algorithms and generative AI are reshaping how people access and trust information, with major effects on journalism, expression, and rights. We foster media literacy and inform digital platform governance.
Culture
As AI transforms how culture is created, accessed, managed, and experienced, UNESCO works to ensure AI’s development and use protect and promote cultural diversity, creativity, and access for all.
Gender
New technologies risk widening gender gaps, especially when AI learns from biased data. UNESCO’s work on AI and gender guides policymakers and innovators to close these divides.
Education
We convene leaders, experts, and innovators to address the impact of AI and technology in education, promoting human-centered, inclusive, and equitable approaches to the benefit of all learners.
Building standards together: emerging technology ethics
UNESCO’s normative recommendations guide the ethical use of technologies, helping ensure they respect human rights, promote fairness, and benefit everyone.
Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology
The 2025 UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology sets global principles to ensure neurotechnology is developed and used in ways that respect human rights, dignity, and societal well-being.
Recommendation on the Ethics of AI
In 2021, UNESCO adopted the Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, guiding its work and helping Member States develop ethically aligned AI policies and capacities.
Policy Development: Readiness Assessment Methodology (RAMs)
UNESCO helps Member States evaluate their readiness for the AI transformation through its Readiness Assessment Methodology (RAM) program, which helps policymakers identify their policy gaps and develop their national policies and strategies toward the development and deployment of these transformative technologies.
As of October 2025, over 75 countries from five continents have initiated or completed to RAM assessments, and policymakers worldwide are further able to draw on the Technology Policy Assistance Facility, developed in cooperation with the South African G20 Presidency.

Key initiatives
G20 Technology Policy Assistance Facility
A G20-backed platform that helps policymakers and stakeholders research, design, and implement ethical, inclusive, and future-ready technology and AI policies.
Global AI Ethics and Governance Observatory
The Observatory supports global stakeholders in promoting ethical and responsible AI through research, tools, and best practices.
Readiness Assessment Methodology (RAM)
The RAM program helps governments identify and address gaps in their AI policies, strategies, and legislation, so that AI is deployed ethically and responsibly to the benefit of their their citizens.
Internet Universality Indicators
This tool helps countries assess their Internet landscape, guide evidence-based policies, and foster inclusive, future-ready digital governance.
UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance
The UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance brings together Member States and stakeholders to engage in the meaningful global conversation on AI that the world needs.
Coordinated by UNESCO and the ITU as the joint UN Secretariat, the Dialogue—mandated by the General Assembly—aims to ensure that AI governance reflects the priorities of all nations, not just the most technologically advanced. International cooperation on AI governance is essential to ensure that AI development benefits all of us.
